newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Political party chief assassinated in Mogadishu.
newsitem.headline: Political party chief assassinated in Mogadishu.

text.p: Gunmen loyal to Somali faction leader Hussein Aideed assassinated a leader of a rival group and killed two other officials on Friday night, party officials said on Saturday.

They said Mohamed Ahmed Nuur, 48, secretary-general of the United Somali Congress-Somali National Alliance (USC-SNA) wing led by Ali Hassan Osman Atto, was killed when his car was ambushed in south Mogadishu.
Another party activist, Mohamed Jama Sofi, was killed in the attack in Medina quarter near south Mogadishu's closed airport.
They said party supporter Mohamed Miradine, was killed on Friday night when gunmen attacked his south Mogadishu home.
In a statement on a radio station operated by Osman Atto's faction, the party said the Friday shootings and other killings in the last month had been carried out by Aideed supporters.
The party vowed to take revenge against a rival USC-SNA wing led by Aideed, a 34-year-old former U.S. marine who succeeded his father Mohamed Farah Aideed when he died in Mogadishu on August 1.
There was no immediate comment from officials loyal to Aideed.
Doctors at a south Mogadishu hospital said on Saturday two other people were killed and a former official in Aideed's government was wounded by gunmen in the city on Friday night.
Some Mogadishu residents believe Osman Atto's supporters assassinated Hussein Aideed's 62-year-old father and loyalists are taking revenge in line with a centuries-old tradition of vendettas.

Hussein Aideed, elected president of Somalia by supporters, and members of his government say Mohamed Farah Aideed died of a heart attack. But his officials initially said he was shot dead by a gunman.
More than 13 people have been killed and 16 wounded in a string of attacks and ambushes in the last two weeks, mostly involving supporters of the two south Mogadishu leaders.
Osman Atto, a financier, broke with Mohamed Farah Aideed last year shortly after the departure of U.N. peacekeeping forces from Somalia. He is currently believed to be in Ethiopia.

Some residents said they feared the vendetta within the same clan would only intensify, bringing more insecurity to a city already abandoned by foreign aid workers because of kidnappings and extortion.
Non-governmental aid agencies suspended "non-vital" operations in the Somali capital Mogadishu on Thursday to press for the release of a kidnapped Somali aid worker seized in north Mogadishu.
Their action followed a decision by U.N. aid agencies to suspend operations from Wednesday if Hilal Aden was not freed.
The aid suspension followed a recommendation from the Somali Aid Coordination Body (SACB), grouping aid agencies and donors. The SACB had called for a shutdown unless Aden was released.
The SACB said Aden, an employee with the Swedish Life and Peace Institute, had been held without proper medical treatment despite being wounded when he was kidnapped on September 19.
